transcript: [00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining. we're on for about an hour, maya from Redwood, and Carlos my SE is here. quick roll call?
[00:06] Lina Park: Lina here, CTO. Ethan here too, and Priya. good to be on.
[00:12] Carlos Ruiz: hey all. excited to dig into the inference econ playbook. we'll go through a few scenarios and a live cost sim.
[00:24] Ethan Ross: quick ask up front — we care about tail latency for our UI flows, 99th under 250ms ideally, also cost per 1M requests is a big gating factor.
[00:35] Maya Chen: perfect, we'll frame the scenarios exactly around that. mind if we start with a quick stack and traffic profile? Priya, you can chime in for infra constraints.
[00:46] Priya Singh: we run on GCP, mostly GKE, some on-prem inference for sensitive data. we have SSO via Okta, KMS for keys, and strict egress rules — VPC peering only.

[00:59] Carlos Ruiz: good context. so two lens: per-token unit economics with batching and caching, and the deployment choices — hosted api vs dedicated reserved capacity vs private/vpc — that affect latency/cost. we'll start with a basic model and then toggle parameters.

[01:18] Maya Chen: quick note, our 'Optimize' suggestions will recommend batch size targets, prefix cache policies, and whether to prefetch KV for sessionized requests. there was a typo in some earlier docs calling it 'KV-cache prefetcher' but same idea.
[01:35] Ethan Ross: what's the difference between prefix cache and session cache? we've heard both terms in other vendors docs and they sounded similar.

[01:44] Carlos Ruiz: good question. prefix cache (we also call it prefix/KV cache) stores KV-cache snapshots for frequent input prefixes — e.g., user prompt templates — so you can skip early transformer layers. session cache is more per-session KV reuse. prefix is higher hit-rate for templated UI prompts. sessionization is better when you have long-running conversations.
[02:12] Lina Park: and prefetching is proactively loading KV for expected next steps?
[02:17] Carlos Ruiz: yes, exactly. prefetching warms the KV for predicted continuation, reducing first-token latency at cost of extra compute/requests. it's a tradeoff in the cost model we show.
[02:30] Maya Chen: i'll share the simple cost equation: total = tokens * cost_per_token - savings_from_cache_and_batching +/- prefetch overhead. we'll demo numbers now.
[02:47] [Screen share starts - Opt deck]

[03:10] Carlos Ruiz: scenario A: interactive chat UI, single-turn median prompt ~80 tokens, expected 200 RPS at peak. with no caching and small batch size, cost baseline X. when we apply continuous batching up to 16, and prefix cache hit rate 18%, you see about 28% reduction in token cost in the model.
[03:41] Priya Singh: is that 18% realistic? our prompts vary a lot — we do have templates but users append free text.

[03:51] Carlos Ruiz: totally — hit rates depend on template adherence. our playbook recommends measuring template overlap and starting with conservative hit rate assumptions, then increase if telemetry shows more reuse. we also simulate a 'mixed template' scenario.
[04:08] Ethan Ross: show me dedicated vs hosted math — how much is reserved capacity worth for our 200 RPS?

[04:15] Maya Chen: in the spreadsheet we ran a committed capacity scenario — for 200 RPS sustained, dedicated GPUs lowered unit cost by around 35% vs hosted on pay-as-you-go in our model, but that assumes you fill the capacity. if you have spiky traffic, hosted or burst configs plus prefix cache might be better.
[04:38] Lina Park: our traffic is spiky: 9am-11am heavy, evenings light. we can't commit to high reserved spend yet. are there autoscale + burst options?

[04:48] Carlos Ruiz: yes. Redwood Dedicated supports autoscaling policies with burst capacity. the Optimize module can recommend buffer sizing and a hybrid policy: base load on dedicated, spill to hosted API during peaks. that keeps steady unit economics while avoiding overcommit.

[05:10] Maya Chen: let's walk through a prefetch trade simulation. imagine a flow where after an initial template, the user triggers a follow-up that we can predict 60% of the time. if you prefetch KV at that 60% probability, you reduce the follow-up latency 1st token by ~120ms on average but incur prefetch compute cost for the 40% misses.

[05:37] Ethan Ross: so the cost equation needs good priors on prediction accuracy. our product team is worried about wasted compute. is there a way to gate prefetching to only high-confidence transitions?

[05:47] Carlos Ruiz: absolutely. in Optimize you can set a prefetch threshold. default is conservative (75% confidence). you can A/B test with canaries, track cost delta and latency improvements, and rollback automatically if cost ratio isn't acceptable.
[06:04] Priya Singh: SSO and network — if we go private VPC, what changes? we need to preserve our KMS and audit requirements.

[06:12] Maya Chen: Private deployment gives you a customer-managed control plane in your VPC or on-prem. KMS integration or HSM works, audit logs are pushed to your logging cluster. our security brief (i'll share) covers SOC2, ISO mappings and network diagrams.
[06:28] Lina Park: do you provide sample network diagrams? our security team always asks for specifics.

[06:32] Carlos Ruiz: yes — we'll attach the VPC peering and private link examples. also note that Private has different latency profiles because it's within your network, usually lower egress latency but higher ops overhead.
[06:50] [10 minute mark - pause for questions]
[06:58] Samir Gupta: curious about tokenization differences — we use a custom tokenizer. does Redwood's runtime support custom tokenizers?

[07:05] Carlos Ruiz: we support custom tokenization, but it affects model alignment and unit cost because token counts change. part of the onboarding we do tokenization baselining and reconcile sample prompts.
[07:22] Maya Chen: okay next, live cost sim. i'll flip to the spreadsheet where we parameterize batch size, prefix hit rate, prefetch probability, and deployment mode.
[07:32] [Screen shows an interactive spreadsheet — numbers change live]

[07:40] Carlos Ruiz: notice when you increase batch size from 1 to 8, latency for median requests moves slightly but throughput and unit cost drop. continuous batching is sensitive to concurrency distribution — if you have very low concurrency, batching offers less benefit.
[08:02] Priya Singh: our concurrency per user session is low, but aggregate concurrency is high. is there smart routing to group compatible requests into batches?

[08:12] Carlos Ruiz: yes, our serving runtime groups requests by model, sequence length, and priority. Optimize will recommend routing rules and per-route batching windows so you don't batch latency-sensitive paths too aggressively.
[08:30] Ethan Ross: any heuristic numbers for enjoying both low latency and cost? like target batch size for 80-token prompts at our 200 RPS?

[08:38] Carlos Ruiz: for 80-token medians at 200 RPS, starting point: batch size 8-12, prefix hit target 15-25% if you have templated content. prefetch enabled for high-confidence transitions. we'll tune in the sandbox.
[09:01] Lina Park: what about KV cache storage — does Redwood charge for cache storage or only compute?

[09:06] Maya Chen: primary cost is compute for KV usage and prefetch compute. storage for cached snapshots is minimal and included in the service; persistent session store options exist for longer-term storage but those may incur additional fees for extremely large states.
[09:22] Carlos Ruiz: also note quantization choices affect runtime memory and KV footprint. if you choose higher quantization, KV sizes shrink which can improve cache hit density.
[09:34] Ethan Ross: security question — audit logs for who queried what prompt? we need detailed logs for compliance.

[09:41] Maya Chen: we can provide token-level anonymized logs, request/response hashes, and request metadata. full PII capture is configurable and we can integrate with your SIEM. this is covered in the SOC2 docs we'll share.
[09:57] Priya Singh: on the sandbox — what's involved? credentials, network, cost?

[10:02] Carlos Ruiz: sandbox is isolated demo environment. we'll provide a test API key or a dedicated sandbox deployment in your account for private tests. it includes a sample load script and prebuilt dataset for your flows. Carlos will send runbook.
[10:18] [Screen demo: batch size slider toggled — cost delta displayed]

[10:33] Maya Chen: quick aside — competitors sometimes recommend aggressive prefetch defaults which can blow up spend. our Optimize default is conservative and includes regression alarms tied to cost delta per hour.
[10:47] Ethan Ross: do you have any customers with similar props where prefetch helped?

[10:51] Maya Chen: yes — retail search UX customer saw 22% drop in 99p latency by prefetching next-step KV in common flows with only a 6% incremental compute cost, net positive economics. we anonymized that case study — can share.
[11:08] Lina Park: let's return to failure modes — what happens if prefetch backfires (e.g., high miss rate) and we suddenly hit cost spikes?
[11:16] Carlos Ruiz: Optimize supports guardrails: prefetch throttles, cost alarms, and automatic rollback. you can also run canaries on a small percentage of traffic before full rollout.
[11:29] Priya Singh: for on-prem or private deployment, who manages ops? we have a relatively small infra team.

[11:35] Maya Chen: Private can be delivered as a managed option where Redwood handles upgrades and runbooks, or as customer-managed if you prefer full control. Managed private includes monitoring integrations and a support SLA.
[11:48] [15 minute mark - customer questions — deeper technical dive begins]
[11:54] Ethan Ross: curious about KV serialization — is it model-specific? do we need to reserialize when we change model versions?

[12:02] Carlos Ruiz: KV format is versioned per model family; when you roll models we provide an automated migration path and tools to reindex cached prefixes. the runtime can fallback to compute path during migration.
[12:21] Maya Chen: important note: rollouts and canaries are first-class in Redwood Console — you can pin model versions and set automatic fallback if performance regresses.
[12:33] Samir Gupta: about quantization — our QA team worries about quality drift. do you run quality monitoring?
[12:40] Carlos Ruiz: yes, Optimize ties to evals. you set a prompt set and baseline quality metrics; if quantized model deviates beyond threshold the rollout is halted and alerted.
[12:56] Priya Singh: any differences in observability between hosted and private? we need full traces and per-token latency breakdowns.
[13:03] Maya Chen: both expose similar telemetry; Private lets you retain logs longer in your storage. Console has token-level cost, route breakdowns, and latency waterfall charts.
[13:18] Ethan Ross: ok final part — let's sketch an initial adoption plan and timeline.

[13:24] Carlos Ruiz: recommended two-phase plan: Phase 1 (2-4 weeks) — baseline sizing, tokenization baseline, and sandbox perf run. Phase 2 (4-8 weeks) — pilot with prefix cache and conservative prefetch on a subset of traffic, then tune. If successful, evaluate Dedicated commit numbers.
[13:44] Maya Chen: i'm noting dependencies: Priya provides traffic histogram, product (Samir) provides primary user flows, and Ethan defines latency vs cost success metrics.
[13:55] Lina Park: sounds good. timeline risk is our year-end freeze, but the sandbox run in January is doable.
[14:05] Maya Chen: recap: we'll send the spreadsheet + security docs, Carlos will schedule the sandbox, and Priya will send traffic profiles. any other blockers?
[14:14] Priya Singh: none from infra, thanks. will do the histogram.
[14:18] Ethan Ross: please include a sample workload for our retail search use-case — helps us validate.
[14:23] Carlos Ruiz: will do — i'll add a prebuilt retail-search workload to the sandbox artifacts.

[14:30] Maya Chen: last note — i've included a short checklist in the shared artifacts: token baseline, request distribution, success metrics, and security checklist. we'll follow up via the CRM. thanks everyone.
[14:42] Lina Park: thanks — end of call.
